The **yellow-eared parrot** (***Ognorhynchus icterotis***) is a [vulnerable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulnerable_species "Vulnerable species") [parrot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parrot "Parrot") found in the [Andes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes "Andes") of [Colombia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombia "Colombia"). It was thought to be extinct up until April 1999, when a group of researchers that were sponsored by ABC and Fundación Loro Parque, discovered a total of 81 individuals in the Colombian Andes.[[3]](#cite_note-3) It is currently enlisted as [vulnerable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulnerable_species "Vulnerable species") on the [International Union for Conservation of Nature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Union_for_Conservation_of_Nature "International Union for Conservation of Nature") (IUCN) Red List. Its current population trend is increasing, in part due to conservation measures implemented to protect the existing populations of the species. It is closely associated with the wax palm (*[Ceroxylon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceroxylon "Ceroxylon")* sp.).

## Description

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Yellow-eared_parrot&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Description")]

The yellow-eared parrot is a relatively large, long-tailed parrot, with an average length of 42 cm (17 in) and a weight of about 285 g (10.1 oz).[[4]](#cite_note-4) It is overall green, with the underparts being paler, more [lime green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lime_(color) "Lime (color)") than the upperparts. The heavy beak and a ring of bare skin around the eyes are black. The origin of the common epithet "yellow-eared" derives from the yellow patch of feathers that extends from the forehead down to its cheeks and ear-coverts. Its calls sound similar to those of geese.[[5]](#cite_note-ourendangeredworld.com-5)

185|The **saiga antelope** (***Saiga tatarica***, [/ˈsaɪɡə/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")) or **saiga** is a species of [antelope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antelope "Antelope") which during [antiquity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_history "Ancient history") inhabited a vast area of the [Eurasian steppe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurasian_steppe "Eurasian steppe"), spanning the foothills of the [Carpathian Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carpathian_Mountains "Carpathian Mountains") in the northwest and [Caucasus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caucasus "Caucasus") in the southwest into Mongolia in the northeast and [Dzungaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dzungaria "Dzungaria") in the southeast. During the [Pleistocene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pleistocene "Pleistocene"), it ranged across the [mammoth steppe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mammoth_steppe "Mammoth steppe") from the British Isles to [Beringia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beringia "Beringia"). Today, the dominant subspecies (*S. t. tatarica*) only occurs in [Kalmykia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalmykia "Kalmykia") and [Astrakhan Oblast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astrakhan_Oblast "Astrakhan Oblast") of Russia and in the [Ural Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ural_Mountains "Ural Mountains"), [Ustyurt Plateau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ustyurt_Plateau "Ustyurt Plateau") and [Betpak-Dala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betpak-Dala "Betpak-Dala") regions of Kazakhstan. A portion of the Ustyurt population migrates south to Uzbekistan and occasionally to Turkmenistan in winter. It is regionally extinct in Romania, Ukraine, Moldova, China and southwestern Mongolia. The Mongolian subspecies (*S. t. mongolica*) occurs only in western Mongolia.[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)

191|The [scientific name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_name "Scientific name") *Capra tatarica* was coined by [Carl Linnaeus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Linnaeus "Carl Linnaeus") in 1766 in the [12th edition of *Systema Naturae*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/12th_edition_of_Systema_Naturae "12th edition of Systema Naturae").[[5]](#cite_note-5) It was reclassified as *Saiga tatarica* and is the sole living member of the [genus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genus_(biology) "Genus (biology)") *Saiga*.[[6]](#cite_note-MSW3-6) Two [subspecies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subspecies "Subspecies") are recognised:[[6]](#cite_note-MSW3-6)[[7]](#cite_note-Groves-7)[[1]](#cite_note-iucn-1)
192|
193|* *S. t. tatarica* (Linnaeus, 1766): also known as the Russian saiga, it is only to be found today in central Asia.
194|* *S. t. mongolica* Bannikov, 1946: also known as the [Mongolian saiga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongolian_saiga "Mongolian saiga"), it is sometimes treated as an independent species, or as subspecies of the [Pleistocene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pleistocene "Pleistocene") *Saiga borealis*;[[1]](#cite_note-iucn-1) it is confined to Mongolia.

196|In 1945, American paleontologist [George Gaylord Simpson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Gaylord_Simpson "George Gaylord Simpson") classified both in the [tribe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tribe_(biology) "Tribe (biology)") Saigini under the same subfamily, [Caprinae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caprinae "Caprinae"). Subsequent authors were not certain about the relationship between the two, until [phylogenetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phylogenetics "Phylogenetics") studies in the 1990s revealed that though morphologically similar, the [Tibetan antelope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibetan_antelope "Tibetan antelope") is closer to the Caprinae while the saiga is closer to the Antilopinae.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

198|In a revision of the [phylogeny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phylogeny "Phylogeny") of the [tribe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tribe_(biology) "Tribe (biology)") [Antilopini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antilopini "Antilopini") on the basis of [nuclear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nucleus_(biology) "Nucleus (biology)") and [mitochondrial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitochondria "Mitochondria") data in 2013, Eva Verena Bärmann (of the [University of Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Cambridge "University of Cambridge")) and colleagues showed that the saiga is [sister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sister_taxon "Sister taxon") to the [clade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clade "Clade") formed by the [springbok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Springbok "Springbok") (*Antidorcas marsupialis*) and the [gerenuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerenuk "Gerenuk") (*Litocranius walleri*).[[9]](#cite_note-barmann-9) The study noted that the saiga and the springbok could be considerably different from the rest of the antilopines; a 2007 phylogenetic study suggested that the two form a clade sister to the gerenuk.[[10]](#cite_note-10) The cladogram below is based on the 2013 study.[[9]](#cite_note-barmann-9)

# Conservation of the Yellow-eared Parrot

![](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5f95e07565cf981a7d24ed98/8bc4310d-2ef0-4847-a812-43a704d4bc37/012+Yellow-eared+Parrot.png)

## **Blueprint**

### **ASSESS**

In 1998, Loro Parque Fundación funded a project to evaluate the last population known in Ecuador as the flock had disappeared unexpectedly. The species was listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species since 1994 and was considered potentially extinct in Ecuador. When re-discovered in Colombia in 1999, there were only an estimated 81 birds. The Fundación began a new assessment project to evaluate the threats to their persistence. The field project found evidence of severe habitat loss, especially related to wax palms (*Ceroxylum quindiuense*) which are preferred by the Yellow-eared Parrot in the area. The wax palm is the world’s tallest palm, is a slow-growing and long-lived species, and is Colombia's national tree. It was logged for pastures and fence posts, but also extensively overharvested for use in religious celebrations.

### **PLAN**

A local NGO, Fundación ProAves, was formed in response to the task of protecting and recovering the remnant Colombian parrot population. They met with local stakeholders and developed a plan that would: 1) secure the habitat by fencing remaining palm groves, 2) implement reforestation, 3) mount artificial nest boxes to boost reproduction, and 4) develop an environmental education programme with the local population. A major objective was to gain support and collaborate with the local community, to both reduce the immediate threats for parrots, but also lead to preserving the whole palm forest ecosystem.

### **ACT**

In 2000, action was taken to increase the number of parrots which could be successfully raised each year. This was done by supplementing the habitat with artificial nest boxes. At the same time, basic ecological and habitat-use studies began to describe the bird’s foraging and roosting needs. These studies mapped the migration corridors between the parrot’s habitat. Zones at high altitude (2,700–3,000 m) were found to be of great relevance for the immediate survival of the parrot, owing to the relatively good conservation status of these forests and because parrots use these areas for all three main behaviors (feeding, nesting, roosting). Nevertheless, the foraging data indicated that lower zones are essential when food is seasonally scarce in the highlands. Critically important vegetation zones were fenced to protect them from grazing livestock. Reforestation in the lower elevations started with a focus on the five most commonly used food plant species, plus the wax palm in which the entire population prefers for communal roosting every evening and nests in its dead trunks. Slowly this habitat restoration began to provide the birds with necessary resources for population expansion.

Awareness-raising activities included poster campaigns, environmental education, community workshops, school visits, and radio broadcasts. Close cooperation with the local community and churches  reduced the need for wax palm leaves during religious events over time. This tradition of use has been reversed and now there are celebratory festivals where wax palm seedlings are planted.

## **Results**

After more than two decades, the Yellow-eared Parrot population has recovered in Colombia and the species now numbers well over 3,800 individuals. Though still threatened, their conservation status has changed to Vulnerable in the IUCN Red List. Two reserves (4,200 hectares) were established where conservation efforts continue for the Yellow-eared Parrot and other species. In 2009, an additional 6,600 hectares was acquired and established a corridor for threatened parrots across the Central Cordillera in Colombia. Currently, Loro Parque Fundación is funding conservation actions to reforest the historic roost site in Ecuador, survey for the species, and secure critical habitat.
